section.title: Final Instructions and Greetings
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes with practical travel plans, the sending of coworkers, provision for Zenas and Apollos, and a final greeting. Yet even here the letter's great theme surfaces one last time: our people must learn to devote themselves to good works, and the closing blessing is simply grace. The mundane and the gospel are woven together.
section.thesis: Even the ordinary logistics of ministry, comings and goings, provision, and greetings, are the setting for a life devoted to fruitful good works, all held together and blessed by the grace that runs through the whole letter.
section.frameNote: Two movements: final instructions about travel, coworkers, and provision, capped by the recurring call to devote our lives to good works so we are not unfruitful; then the closing greetings and the benediction of grace to all.

units.label: Travel plans and provision
units.note: learn to do good and be fruitful

verses.text: As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, {{spoudazo|make every effort}} to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there.
Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need.
And our people must also learn to devote themselves to {{kalaerga|good works}} in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful.
All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. {{charis|Grace}} be with all of you.

spoudazo.gloss: To make every effort, to be diligent, to hasten. It conveys eager, purposeful haste. Paul uses it for Titus coming to Nicopolis and, closely related, for the diligent equipping of Zenas and Apollos. Even ordinary ministry arrangements are to be pursued with earnest care, not casual indifference.

kalaerga.gloss: Good works, literally beautiful or excellent deeds. The phrase is a drumbeat through Titus, and here believers must learn to devote themselves to such works to meet urgent needs. Good works are not optional extras but the ordinary fruit of grace, so that the redeemed life is a useful, fruitful one.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's undeserved favour in Christ. The letter opened with grace, verse 1:4, and now closes with it: grace be with all of you. Grace both frames and fills the letter, the source of salvation in chapters 2 and 3 and the final word of blessing over the whole church.

basic.context: Paul wraps up the letter with practical matters: he will send Artemas or Tychicus so Titus can join him at Nicopolis for the winter, and Titus should generously supply Zenas and Apollos for their journey. Then, one more time, Paul urges God's people to devote themselves to good works so their lives bear fruit. He closes with greetings and a blessing of grace.
basic.hermeneutics: These closing verses are real history, naming real people and places, which reminds us the letter is grounded in actual ministry. Even so, Paul cannot sign off without returning to his great theme of good works, showing that doctrine is meant to land in everyday, useful service. The final word, grace, echoes the letter's opening.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul urges Titus to spoudazo, to make every effort, to come, and to do his best to equip the travellers. Believers must learn to devote themselves to kala erga, good works, literally beautiful deeds, so they are not unfruitful. The letter ends as it began, with charis, grace, be with all.
basic.typology: The naming of ordinary coworkers and the call to meet pressing needs reflect the body of Christ at work, each member supplying what others lack, a living picture of the mutual care that marks God's people in every age.
basic.christ: Though Christ is not named in these final verses, the grace that blesses the church is His grace, the grace whose appearing in Jesus the whole letter has celebrated. The good works urged here flow from the people He redeemed and purified for Himself.
basic.god: God's grace is the first and last word over His people. He cares about practical provision, fruitful lives, and the bonds of love among believers, showing that He is Lord of the ordinary as well as the eternal.
basic.crossReferences: Second Timothy 4 shows Paul similarly arranging coworkers and travel. Acts 18 introduces Apollos, an eloquent teacher of the Scriptures. And Philippians 4 shows the same care to meet one another's pressing needs.
basic.oneStory: The letter ends where it began, in grace, framing all its instruction. Ordinary logistics become the arena for a fruitful, good-works life among a people saved by grace. It is a small window on the whole story: a redeemed community, cared for and blessed by grace, living usefully in the world until Christ appears.

context.literary:
These four verses are short, yet they are carefully built as the closing movement of a letter that has been about order, sound teaching and grace. They fall into three small units. Verses 12 and 13 are about people on the move: Artemas or Tychicus will come to Crete, Titus is to join Paul, and Zenas and Apollos are to be supplied for their journey. Verse 14 turns from the individuals to the whole community, in a sentence that begins with the word also, and says that our people must learn to devote themselves to good works. Verse 15 closes with greetings and a benediction.

The pieces are linked by echoes of the opening of the letter. In 1:5 Paul says he left Titus to set in order the things that were lacking, and in 3:13 Titus is to make sure that Zenas and Apollos lack nothing, with the same root. In 1:4 the letter begins with grace and peace, and in 3:15 it ends with grace. In 1:16 the false teachers are unfit for any good deed, and in 3:14 the believers are to learn to devote themselves to good works. The letter has come full circle.

The most striking feature is the verb devote in verse 14, which is the same verb as in 3:8. The statement in verse 8, that believers should take care to devote themselves to good deeds, is now repeated at the end as the heart of what the letter has been teaching, with the added phrase to meet pressing needs. Paul gives the final word on the subject in the form of a practical instruction.
context.historical:
Paul's plan to winter at Nicopolis tells us something about the situation of the letter. The best known city of that name lay on the western coast of Greece, in Epirus, and had been founded by Augustus after his victory at Actium, which gave it the meaning city of victory. It was a thriving harbour town and a convenient place for a missionary to spend the months when sea travel was closed, as in Acts 27:12 and 28:11. Paul had made similar winter plans in 1 Corinthians 16:6. The travel does not fit within Acts, which is one reason many place Titus after Paul's release from the imprisonment at the end of Acts, in the first half of the 60s, though not everyone accepts this setting.

The named people were known workers. Tychicus appears as a trusted helper in Acts 20:4, as the bearer of Ephesians and Colossians, Ephesians 6:21-22 and Colossians 4:7-9, and as someone sent to Ephesus in 2 Timothy 4:12. Artemas is named only here. Apollos was the eloquent Alexandrian Jew who taught the Scriptures accurately in Acts 18:24-28 and whom Paul urged to visit Corinth in 1 Corinthians 16:12. Zenas is called a lawyer, which may mean an expert in the Jewish law or a Roman legal practitioner.

There is a further detail. In 2 Timothy 4:10, Paul says Titus has gone to Dalmatia, a region across the Adriatic from Italy and north of Epirus, which fits a movement of Titus from Crete to join Paul at Nicopolis and onward. Paul's request to do his best to come before winter in 2 Timothy 4:21 is also in the same language as Titus 3:12. Travellers in the ancient world depended on the hospitality and gifts of local believers, so supplying couriers was a serious ministry.
context.canonical:
The ending of Titus stands in a long line of Pauline closings. Romans 16 and Colossians 4 hold longer lists of greetings, while the personal notes at the end of 2 Timothy 4 are closest in tone to this one. These endings are not filler. They show that the letters were written out of a network of friendships and shared labour, with couriers, hosts and fellow workers, and that the gospel travelled along those lines of trust.

The call to good works that closes the letter picks up one of its main themes and joins it to the rest of the Bible's teaching on caring for people in need. Paul urged believers to remember the poor in Galatians 2:10, and the same Titus was involved in the collection for the believers in Jerusalem, 2 Corinthians 8:6 and 8:16-24. Ephesians 4:28 asks that a person who steals should work so as to have something to share with the needy. Romans 12:13 asks believers to contribute to the needs of the saints and to practise hospitality, and 1 John 3:17-18 says love must show itself in deed and in truth.

The image of fruit has a long history. Psalm 1 describes the blessed person as a tree that yields fruit in its season, and Isaiah 5 portrays Israel as a vineyard that produced bad grapes. Jesus says that every branch in Him that bears no fruit is taken away, John 15:2, and Paul prays that believers will bear fruit in every good work, Colossians 1:10. The phrase that they will not be unfruitful is a final reminder that real faith bears fruit in useful works.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul has two aims in these closing lines, one immediate and one lasting. The immediate aim is practical. He wants Titus to come to him once a replacement arrives, so that the work on Crete is not left without leadership, and he wants two gospel workers, Zenas and Apollos, to be sent on their way properly provided for. The churches would be expected to help, and Titus is the one who must see that they do.

The lasting aim is in the middle of the passage. Paul has told the Cretan believers that their salvation was by mercy and not works, and he has told them that they must be ready for every good work. In verse 14 he says it again to the whole church, not only to leaders, as a thing to be learned: our people must learn to devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs. The word learn suggests that goodness is a habit that is formed and not just a feeling. It also gives a reason, that they will not be unfruitful. Paul wants a church that is useful, and he sees ordinary generosity as the place where grace shows itself.

Finally, he sends greetings and a blessing in the plural. Though the letter is addressed to Titus, it is meant to be heard by the congregations, and the farewell reaches them all.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The travel plans are descriptive. They record what Paul intended at a particular time and do not give a rule that anyone should winter at a certain city or send particular individuals to a certain place. What carries over is the principle underneath them, that gospel workers deserve to be sent on their way and supplied with what they need, which Paul teaches in several places, including 1 Corinthians 9:14 and 3 John 5-8.

The command in verse 14 is prescriptive. Believers are to learn to devote themselves to good works, particularly to meeting pressing needs, so that they are not unfruitful. This is not a call for activism or a way to earn favour, since the letter has just insisted that salvation is by mercy. It is the proper response of people who have received grace. The needs in view are real, practical needs, and the church is the community that meets them. The greetings are descriptive but still instructive: the church is meant to be a web of affection, with believers who love one another in the faith.

debates.question: Where is Nicopolis, and what does the plan tell us about the letter's date?

views.label: Nicopolis in Epirus, after Paul's release
views.case: The most famous city of that name was on the western coast of Greece, and several ancient sources describe it as a place where travellers stayed for the winter. If Paul wintered there after the end of Acts, as 2 Timothy and Titus seem to imply, it fits with a ministry after his first imprisonment in Rome.

views.label: Another Nicopolis, or an earlier setting
views.case: A few ancient cities carried the name, and some suggest a different location or a timeline earlier than the end of Acts. Others, who doubt that Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters, see the travel notes as a literary device. These views are not supported by clear evidence in the text.

debates.bearing: The case for Epirus is strong, and nothing in the letter's teaching depends on the choice. The travel notes show the letter as a real piece of correspondence between colleagues, whatever view one takes of its setting.

debates.question: Who was Zenas the lawyer?

views.label: An expert in the Jewish law
views.case: The Greek word nomikos is used in the Gospels for those who knew the law of Moses, as in Luke 10:25, and the word law is used in the same letter in 3:9. Zenas may have been a Jewish convert trained in Scripture, travelling with Apollos, who was also skilled in the Scriptures.

views.label: A Roman legal professional
views.case: His name is Greek, and the word could also describe someone who practised civil law. A lawyer of this kind would have been a useful ally in a society where Christians faced legal disputes and would bring a different set of gifts to the mission.

debates.bearing: The name appears only here, and the text does not tell us. The point Paul makes is not his profession but that he and Apollos must be generously provided for.

debates.question: What does 'pressing needs' include?

views.label: The material needs of others
views.case: The phrase to meet pressing needs most naturally refers to the urgent needs of people in the community, such as food, shelter and support, as in Ephesians 4:28 and 1 John 3:17. Good works are those that relieve such needs.

views.label: The needs of the ministry as well
views.case: In the context, Paul has just asked Titus to supply travelling workers, so the needs may include the practical support of gospel workers, as in 3 John 5-8 and Philippians 4:16-18. On this reading, good works include generosity toward those who carry the message.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not in conflict. The community that supplies Zenas and Apollos is the same community that meets the needs of its neighbours, and both belong to the life of a fruitful church.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 begins with a command that carries urgency: spoudazo means to make haste or to be diligent, and Paul uses the same verb when he asks Timothy to do his best to come before winter in 2 Timothy 4:9 and 4:21. It is in the aorist imperative, a call for prompt action. The verb for winter, paracheimazo, means to spend the winter, and it occurs in 1 Corinthians 16:6 and Acts 27:12 and 28:11, so it is part of Paul's travel vocabulary.

In verse 13 the BSB says equip, and the Greek verb is propempo, which means to send on one's way and was the word used of helping missionaries with provisions, money and companions for the next stage of a journey. It is found in Acts 15:3, Romans 15:24, 1 Corinthians 16:6 and 16:11, and in 3 John 6, where John says that those who are sent forth in a manner worthy of God should be helped. Paul adds a purpose clause: so that they lack nothing. The verb here is leipo, the root of the word for unfinished in 1:5, so the letter frames the whole assignment as a matter of completing what is lacking.

The phrase good works, kala erga, appears in 3:8 and 3:14, and the adjective kalos can mean good, beautiful or fine. It is not the same word as agathos, though they overlap, and it often refers to what is admirable to an observer. Paul's concern with the church's reputation makes this fitting. The verb devote, proistemi, appears in 3:8 and 3:14. The two uses of the verb in a few verses make it the thread of the second half of the chapter. Its meaning is to stand before, to lead, to manage and to care for, and it is applied to a father managing his household in 1 Timothy 3:4. The believers are to be managers of good works.

The word for needs is chreia, and it is joined with anagkaios, which means necessary or urgent, so the phrase refers to needs that cannot wait. The verb learn, manthano, is in the imperative, and the word akarpos, unfruitful, belongs to the language of the garden and vineyard, used by Jesus in the parable of the sower, Mark 4:19, and by Paul in Ephesians 5:11.

Verse 15 contains two words of affection. The verb greet, aspazomai, is the standard word of greeting and good wishes, and the phrase those who love us in the faith uses phileo, the verb of friendship. The final blessing is the plural of you, meta panton hymon, with all of you, which shows the congregations in view.

typology.fulfillment: Jesus sent His disciples out two by two, Mark 6:7, and appointed seventy two to go ahead of Him in pairs, Luke 10:1. They were to depend on the hospitality of those who received them, Luke 10:7. The sending of Zenas and Apollos, and the supplying of Artemas or Tychicus, continues that pattern: gospel workers travel, and local believers provide for them. It is a pattern more than a type in the strict sense, and the escalation is that the apostles now go with the full account of Christ's death and resurrection. The pattern falls short of fulfilment because the work of the workers is not complete until the whole world has heard.

When Moses asked Israel to give for the tabernacle, everyone whose heart stirred brought an offering, and the workers soon had more than enough, Exodus 35:20-29 and 36:5-7. The generosity of Israel supplied the place where God would dwell among them. In Titus the same willingness is asked for the living temple, the church, which Paul describes as God's temple in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and Ephesians 2:21-22. Giving that keeps gospel workers equipped builds that temple. The correspondence is not exact, since the tabernacle was a building and the church is a people, but both are built by hearts moved by God.

typology.type: The fruitful tree and the vine
typology.fulfillment: Psalm 1:3 describes the one who delights in the law of the Lord as a tree that yields its fruit in its season, and Isaiah 5:1-7 describes Israel as a vineyard that produced wild grapes. Jesus claims to be the true vine and calls His people to bear much fruit by remaining in Him, John 15:1-5. Paul's phrase that they not be unfruitful belongs to this picture. Israel failed to bear what God looked for, and Christ, the faithful vine, makes His people fruitful. The image has its limit: a vine bears fruit from its own life, while the believers' fruit is the product of the life of another.

God gave Aaron and his sons a benediction to place His name on Israel: the Lord bless you and keep you, make His face shine on you and be gracious to you, Numbers 6:24-26. The closing of the letter with grace be with all of you is the apostolic counterpart. It does not wish for a vague good; it asks for the favour of God that has appeared in Christ. The priestly blessing prefigures it, and what the priests could only ask for, Christ has given, 2 Corinthians 13:14. Yet the blessing in the letter remains a prayer until the day of His appearing, when grace is seen in full.

study.christ:
Christ is not named in these closing lines, but He is present in all of them, as the one whose work the letter has described and whose grace it ends by invoking. Grace be with all of you is the blessing of the Lord Jesus, and Paul usually makes it explicit elsewhere, as in Romans 16:20 and 1 Corinthians 16:23. In Titus the grace of the ending recalls the grace of 2:11 that has appeared. A reader who has gone through the whole letter will hear in the last word the name of the one who gave Himself for us to redeem and to purify, 2:14.

The good works that these verses ask of the church are His works in His people. Jesus is described in Acts 10:38 as the one who went about doing good and healing, so the people who devote themselves to good works are following Him. The phrase meet pressing needs reaches back to the gospels, where He feeds the hungry, welcomes strangers and tells His followers that what they do for the least of His brothers they do for Him, Matthew 25:34-40. Paul grounds giving in the example of Christ in 2 Corinthians 8:9: though He was rich, for our sake He became poor, so that through His poverty we might become rich. The Titus whom Paul sent to Corinth to encourage generous giving now teaches the Cretans the same.

The sending of the workers also looks to Christ. He is the sent one, and He sends His people as the Father sent Him, John 20:21. Those who supply Zenas and Apollos share in His mission. The statement in 3 John 7 that the missionaries went out for the sake of the Name shows what is at stake: the support of gospel workers is support of the proclamation of Christ.

Finally, the call to be fruitful brings us to His own words in John 15. Fruitfulness is a result of abiding in Him. The good works of Titus 3:14 are not the believers' attempt to earn their place but the evidence of life in the vine. We should avoid reading more into the names and places than the text allows, since Artemas and Zenas are not symbols. What these verses show is the shape of a church that has understood what Christ has done and now lives on the practical side of it.
study.god:
The ending of Titus shows God as the Lord of the ordinary. The verses deal with travel plans, supplies and greetings, and nothing in them is miraculous. Yet they are part of an inspired letter, which means that the God who inspires doctrine is also concerned with how a courier is provisioned and how a winter is spent. He works through logistics. The gospel's advance on Crete depends in part on the willingness of believers to make sure that others lack nothing.

He is a God who provides through His people. The needs of gospel workers are met by the church, and the pressing needs of the community are met by the church. God does not usually drop supplies from heaven; He gives to some so that they can give to others, as in 2 Corinthians 9:8-11. The call to devote ourselves to good works is therefore a call to be the means of His providence.

He is a God who wants fruitfulness. The word unfruitful carries a warning, and the picture of a tree or vine that bears no fruit suggests that God looks for a result. But the fruit is not forced. It is the natural result of grace, and the same God who requires it supplies it, Philippians 1:11 and 2:13. His character is shown in the way He wants His people to be useful, not for show but because love acts.

He is a God of relationships. The long list of names in Paul's letters, and the short one here, show that He saves a people and binds them together. Verse 15 speaks of those who love us in the faith, and the believer's love for fellow believers is not an optional extra. The faith is a family.

He is a God of grace from first to last. The letter began with grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior, 1:4, and ends with grace. In between, grace has appeared, trained us, saved us and made us heirs. For worship, the passage reminds us to bring everyday matters under the rule of grace, to give thanks for those who have supported the work of the gospel, and to ask for the grace of God to be with our church, not just us as individuals.

crossReferences.note: Paul asks Timothy to do his best to come to him soon, mentions Tychicus whom he has sent to Ephesus, and asks for his cloak and books. It is the same kind of closing as Titus 3:12-13, with travel, couriers and personal requests, and it shows the human side of Paul's ministry.

Paul mentions that Titus has gone to Dalmatia. This detail helps place Titus 3:12, because it shows Titus moving on from Crete to join Paul's circle, and so confirms that the plan to meet at Nicopolis was carried out in some form.

Luke introduces Apollos, a learned and eloquent Jew from Alexandria who knew the Scriptures well and spoke boldly about Jesus, and who was instructed more accurately by Priscilla and Aquila. It gives background to the Apollos of Titus 3:13 and shows why he was worth equipping.

Paul says he urged Apollos to visit the Corinthians with the brothers, but that Apollos was not at all willing to go then and would go when he had opportunity. It shows that Apollos was an independent colleague, not a subordinate, and that Paul respected his judgment.

Paul sends Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister, to tell the Ephesians how he is and to encourage their hearts. It shows the reliability of the person who might come to Crete and why he could be trusted to take over Titus's work.

John commends Gaius for his faithful care for travelling brothers and says to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God, because they went out for the sake of the Name. It uses the same verb as Titus 3:13 and gives the reason for supporting gospel workers.

Paul describes the generosity of the Macedonian churches and the part Titus played in the collection, and he points to the grace of the Lord Jesus who became poor for us. It shows Titus's own history of organising giving, and gives the gospel basis for the good works of Titus 3:14.

The thief must stop stealing and work honestly, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need. It describes the turn from taking to giving, and matches the call in Titus 3:14 to meet pressing needs as part of the new life.

Paul prays that the Colossians will walk worthily, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God. This is the positive side of Titus 3:14, where believers are to be fruitful in good works, and it shows that fruitfulness comes through knowing God.

The letter opens with grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior. Set beside the closing grace in 3:15, it forms a frame around the whole letter, and the sound doctrine, appointed elders, godly households and good works lie between these two mentions of grace.

study.oneStory:
The closing of Titus looks small, but it belongs to the largest story of all. From the beginning God has made a people for Himself and placed them in a world where they have work to do. In Eden, Adam and Eve were put in the garden to work it and keep it, Genesis 2:15. After the fall, work became hard, and the story of Israel is of a people called to be a blessing to the nations, Genesis 12:3, but who often turned inward. The prophets complained that God's people neglected the poor and the stranger, and they promised a day when the Lord would raise up a people who would do justice and love kindness, Micah 6:8.

Christ came and made such a people. In Titus 2:14 He gave Himself to purify for Himself a people zealous for good deeds. The ending of the letter is that people at work in a small way: sending workers, supplying them, caring for needs, and greeting one another. The apostolic network of couriers, hosts and fellow workers is the first form of what the church has been ever since, a worldwide family bound by the gospel and by practical love.

The call to be fruitful gathers up one of the Bible's major images. From the tree of life in the garden, to the blessed tree of Psalm 1, to the vineyard of Isaiah, to the true vine of John 15, the story is about fruit that God looks for in His people. Revelation 22:2 shows the end: the tree of life on each side of the river, yielding its fruit every month, and the leaves for the healing of the nations. The believers' good works are small seeds of that harvest, and Jesus says that even a cup of cold water given in His name will not lose its reward, Matthew 10:42.

The last word of the letter, grace, is the first and the last word of the Bible's story as it reaches its end, since Revelation closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus be with all, Revelation 22:21. The grace that Paul asks for the Cretan churches is the grace in which the whole story ends, and it sustains the people who wait for the appearing of the great God and Savior.

sermon.title: Ordinary People and Everyday Events
sermon.why: The closing message of Begg's series A Study in Titus, expounding Titus 3:12-15, shows how the letter's grand gospel themes come to rest in ordinary names, travel plans, and the call to fruitful good works, sealed by grace. A fitting, orthodox treatment of this final movement.

quiz.q: Why does Paul want Titus to come to Nicopolis?

options.text: Paul has decided to winter there and sends a replacement so Titus can join him.
options.note: Verse 12 explains the plan to send Artemas or Tychicus and meet at Nicopolis.

options.text: To abandon the churches in Crete for good.
options.note: Paul sends a replacement first; the work in Crete is not abandoned.

options.text: Because Titus was in trouble and needed rescue.
options.note: The text gives ministry coordination, not rescue, as the reason.

options.text: To put Titus on trial.
options.note: There is no hint of a trial; it is a ministry rendezvous.

quiz.q: What does Paul ask concerning Zenas and Apollos?

options.text: That Titus diligently equip them so they lack nothing for their journey.
options.note: Verse 13 calls for generous provision of the travelling workers.

options.text: That Titus turn them away as false teachers.
options.note: They are trusted coworkers to be supported, not opposed.

options.text: That Titus ignore their needs.
options.note: The opposite; he is to see they have everything they need.

options.text: That Titus report them to the authorities.
options.note: Paul asks for their support, not their exposure.

quiz.q: What must God's people learn to do, according to verse 14?

options.text: Devote themselves to good works to meet pressing needs, so as not to be unfruitful.
options.note: Verse 14 sounds the letter's theme of fruitful good works once more.

options.text: Focus only on their own comfort.
options.note: The call is to meet others' pressing needs, not self-comfort.

options.text: Withdraw from all practical service.
options.note: Paul urges active, need-meeting good works, not withdrawal.

options.text: Earn salvation through their works.
options.note: Good works flow from grace already received, not to earn salvation.

quiz.q: How does the letter to Titus close?

options.text: With greetings and the blessing, grace be with all of you.
options.note: Verse 15 ends with mutual greetings and the benediction of grace.

options.text: With a stern final warning and no blessing.
options.note: There are warnings earlier, but the letter closes with grace.

options.text: With a long list of Paul's achievements.
options.note: The close is greetings and grace, not self-commendation.

options.text: With no ending at all.
options.note: It ends with a clear greeting and benediction of grace.

quiz.q: What does it show that the letter opens and closes with grace?

options.text: Grace frames and fills the whole letter, the source and seal of the Christian life.
options.note: Grace in 1:4 and 3:15 brackets everything Paul teaches.

options.text: That grace is only a polite formality.
options.note: Grace is the letter's living theme, not mere politeness.

options.text: That good works have replaced grace.
options.note: Good works flow from grace; they do not replace it.

options.text: That the ending is unrelated to the rest.
options.note: The closing grace deliberately echoes the letter's opening and heart.

questions: Paul weaves the gospel into travel plans and provision for coworkers. How might God be inviting you to see your ordinary logistics and errands as arenas for serving Him?
Believers are to learn to devote themselves to good works. What is one pressing need around you that you could actually help meet this week?
Paul warns against being unfruitful. Where do you sense your faith has grown passive, and what would fruitfulness look like there?
The church supported Zenas and Apollos so they lacked nothing. Who are the gospel workers you could be generously supporting right now?
The letter begins and ends with grace. How would resting more deeply in God's grace change the way you serve, give, and relate to others?

translationNotes.note: Nicopolis most likely refers to the city in Epirus on the Adriatic coast, a natural base from which to winter and coordinate onward mission.
Zenas is called a lawyer, either an expert in Jewish law or a Roman jurist; he and Apollos were probably carrying this letter and needed provision for the road.
Some manuscripts (BYZ and TR) add Amen at the end, as the BSB footnote notes; the earliest witnesses close simply with grace be with all of you.
